title: João Pedro Campos
text:
I’m a PhD researcher at UFMG, affiliated with the University of Bristol, working at the intersection of probabilistic graphical models, Bayesian network inference, and explainable AI. Strong background in systems engineering, machine learning, deep learning, and optimization, including non-linear and linear programming. On the applied side, I build end-to-end machine learning systems.
My central research interest is making interpretable decisions with probabilistic models. .

title: My Paper Explained: MAGABN
text: This is the first post in a series where I explain my own papers in plain language. First up: Multi-Agent Genetic Algorithm for Bayesian Networks Structural Learning, published in Knowledge-Based Systems (2025).

title: My Paper Explained: MAGABN
text:
The problem in one sentence
A Bayesian network is a graph that captures how variables influence each other — great for reasoning under uncertainty, and readable by humans. The hard part is drawing that graph from data: given a table of observations, which arrows should connect which variables?

title: My Paper Explained: MAGABN
text:
Why it’s hard
It’s a NP-hard problem. The number of possible graphs explodes as you add variables — far too many to check one by one. So we don’t search for the perfect graph directly. Instead we do search and score: define a score that says “how well does this graph explain the data?” (I use the BIC score), and then go hunting for a graph with a good score. The whole game becomes a smart search through an astronomically large space.

title: My Paper Explained: MAGABN
section: The idea: a neighborhood of solutions
text:
The idea: a neighborhood of solutions
Genetic algorithms are a classic way to run that search: keep a population of candidate graphs, let the good ones “reproduce,” add a little random mutation, repeat. Over generations, quality improves.
Our idea is to improve evolution with an idea borrowed from multi-agent systems. Instead of one big pool where the best solution can quickly take over, I place each candidate graph on a grid and let each one interact only with its immediate neighbors.
That small constraint has a nice effect: a single strong solution can’t instantly dominate the whole population. Good ideas spread gradually, and diversity survives longer. In practice, that means the search is less likely to get stuck in a mediocre local optimum. I call the method MAGABN.

title: My Paper Explained: MAGABN
text:
How it actually works
Three ingredients:

Crossover — two neighboring graphs “mate.” Edges they agree on are passed to the child; edges they disagree on are inherited at random. The better child survives.
Mutation — pick two nodes at random and shake things up: add, remove, or flip the arrow between them. This injects the randomness that keeps the search alive.
Self-learning — every generation, the current best graph gets a focused local polish, a mini-search around it to squeeze out extra quality.

One catch: Bayesian networks can’t contain cycles, and crossover or mutation can accidentally create one. So whenever that happens, a repair step breaks the cycle by removing or reversing an offending edge.

title: My Paper Explained: MAGABN
text:
Did it work?
I tested MAGABN against three well-known methods — a classic genetic algorithm, a particle-swarm approach (BNCPSO), and hill-climbing with tabu search — on three standard benchmark networks (ASIA, CHILD, INSURANCE), across different amounts of data.
The short version: MAGABN was both more accurate and more consistent. It had the best average structure-recovery score in 6 of 8 settings, and the most stable results (lowest variance) in 6 of 8. A statistical test (ANOVA + Tukey) confirmed the edge over the other methods was real, not luck. It held up especially well on the larger networks, which are exactly the cases where structure learning usually struggles.

title: My Paper Explained: MAGABN
text:
The takeaway
A metaheuristic originally built for continuous numerical optimization can be adapted into a reliable learner for a hard combinatorial problem.
If you want the full details, tables, and proofs of significance, the paper is here.
